extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political economy; educated readers and policymakers interested in theories of wages, capital, and economic method
extracted.subtask_description: Critical examination of the classical wage-fund doctrine and the relation of wages, capital, and interest; defines key terms and lays out methodological requirements for political economy. The chapter argues wages are drawn from the product of labor, not from pre-existing capital, and tests theories against facts and first principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political economy must explain poverty amid progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Political economy should give an answer to the question why poverty persists amid advancing wealth — an explanation consistent with the science's teachings and persuasive to the great masses of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter opens by framing as the central problem: 'seek the law which associates poverty with progress, and increases want with advancing wealth.' The explanation must reconcile with other economic truths and withstand tests; it should be communicable to and convincing of public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political economy as a science: identify cause and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Political economy is a science which, in the sequence of certain phenomena, seeks to trace mutual relations and to identify cause and effect, analogous to the physical sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological tests include comparing societies with different conditions and, by imagination, separating/combining/adding/eliminating known forces or factors. The text emphasizes grounding reasoning on firm premises/axioms and applying induction from observed facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept authority; test accepted theories by first principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepted doctrines and authoritative statements must be interrogated from first principles rather than assumed; false premises or overlooked factors should be exposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author proposes to 'take nothing for granted, but to bring even accepted theories to the test of first principles.' This includes a willingness to follow truth regardless of prejudice and to re-examine premises underlying established doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wage-fund (current) doctrine: wages fixed by ratio of labor to capital
rubrics_metrics.description: The current political economy doctrine holds that wages are fixed by the ratio between the number of laborers and the amount of capital devoted to their employment, tending to a minimum sufficient for living because labor tends to increase and overtake capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the dominant theory in textbooks and universities (sometimes called the wage-fund theory). The chapter treats it as a formal doctrine to be examined, noting its widespread acceptance and influence on policy debates (e.g., protectionism, restriction of competition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical test: wages and interest should be inversely related under wage-fund theory
rubrics_metrics.description: If wages depend on the ratio of labor to capital, high wages (scarcity of labor) should coincide with low interest (abundance of capital), and low wages with high interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter tests the theory against facts and finds the opposite: wages and interest tend to move together (both high in new countries, both low in depressions). Example: California historically had both very high wages and very high interest rates. The inconsistency of co-movement is used as an empirical refutation of the wage-fund explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative reconciliation (Cairnes): greater proportion of capital paid in wages in new countries
rubrics_metrics.description: Professor Cairnes' attempted reconciliation: in new countries more of the capital used in production is devoted to payment of wages (less tied up in fixed machinery/material), so even if capital is scarcer wages may be higher because a larger share of capital goes to wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cairnes' example: an old-country manufacture might allocate $80,000 to buildings/machinery and $20,000 to wages, whereas a new-country agricultural outlay of $30,000 might leave $25,000 for wages. The chapter notes this as an attempted explanation but signals it rests on misunderstanding of labor-capital relations and will be challenged later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: wages are drawn from the product of the labor, not from capital
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's central proposition: 'wages, instead of being drawn from capital, are in reality drawn from the product of the labor for which they are paid.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a crucial reversal: wages are the earnings or 'makings' of labor. Payment in money or prior coincidence of money supply does not make wages advances of capital; rather wages represent the portion of the product that labor has already added to the general stock of wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of assuming wages are drawn from capital (doctrines to be rejected if false)
rubrics_metrics.description: If wages are thought to be drawn from capital, a number of doctrines follow: industry is limited by capital; capital must be accumulated before labor is employed; conversion of circulating into fixed capital reduces the fund for maintaining labor; more laborers can be employed at low than high wages; capital applied to agriculture will maintain more laborers than in manufactures; profits relate inversely to wages, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter argues that these consequences form a vast superstructure built on the wage-from-capital premise; demonstrating the premise false would cause these attendant doctrines to fall. The list functions as a map of what is at stake methodologically and politically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production precedes enjoyment; wages are earnings (earning = making)
rubrics_metrics.description: In exchange-based, divided production, what a person receives in return for exertion is truly the product of that exertion; wages represent the 'makings' of labor—the laborer's direct contribution to the general stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations (fisherman, canoe-maker, draughtsman, miner): through exchange each participant effectively produces the goods he consumes; money or drafts represent claims on the product of labor, not pre-existing capital advances for maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive (fact-based) testing over purely deductive reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: To refute entrenched fallacies, switch from deductive argument (from assumed premises) to inductive inquiry beginning with facts and tracing their relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explicitly proposes to 'beginning with facts and tracing their relations' to see if the same conclusions follow as from first principles. This is posited as necessary to meet and overthrow fallacies entrenched by authority and plausible deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insistence on precise definitions (avoid ambiguous usage of terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear and precise definitions of key terms ('wealth,' 'capital,' 'rent,' 'wages,' etc.) are essential in economic reasoning; indistinct usage produces ambiguity and error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter warns that different writers use terms in different senses (and even change senses themselves). The author will state the intended meaning whenever a term becomes important and adhere to that sense throughout to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'wages' (political-economy sense: all returns for exertion)
rubrics_metrics.description: In political economy, 'wages' means the part of the produce that goes to labor and includes all returns for exertion, not only manual labor or payment by an employer; it covers returns to self-employed labor as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: farmer's own produce = his wages; gold washed by self-employed digger = wages; retail profits may include wages (recompense of labor). The author stresses this broader, technical sense even where it is later ignored by standard works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adam Smith's broad definition of capital (eight-fold list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adam Smith: capital of an individual/nation consists of (1) machines and instruments of trade; (2) buildings (instruments of trade); (3) improvements of land; (4) acquired useful abilities of inhabitants; (5) money; (6) provisions in hands of producers/dealers; (7) material or partially completed manufactured articles in hands of producers/dealers; (8) completed articles in hands of producers/dealers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith distinguishes fixed capital (first four) and circulating capital (last four). This listing is given to show the divergence among authorities over what 'capital' denotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ricardo's definition of capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Ricardo: 'Capital is that part of the wealth of a country which is employed in production, and consists of food, clothing, tools, raw materials, machinery, etc., necessary to give effect to labor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ricardo's definition differs from Smith's by excluding some items Smith included and including some Smith excluded (e.g., food/clothing in possession of consumer). The text uses these differing canonical definitions to highlight ambiguity in the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: McCulloch's definition of capital
rubrics_metrics.description: McCulloch: 'The capital of a nation really comprises all those portions of the produce of industry existing in it that may be directly employed either to support human existence or to facilitate production.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition follows Ricardo's line but is wider; it includes anything capable of aiding production regardless of actual use (e.g., a pleasure carriage horse might be capital because it could be used for plowing if needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mill's definition of capital (determination to use as test)
rubrics_metrics.description: John Stuart Mill: 'Whatever things are destined to supply productive labor with the shelter, protection, tools and materials which the work requires, and to feed and otherwise maintain the laborer during the process, are capital.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill emphasizes the determination to use as the test of capital (i.e., things destined for productive use), distinguishing capital by intended purpose rather than strict capability or current use.
